ie-01.title: Systems view: inputs, transformation, outputs
explain: **Industrial engineering** treats the flow of work, in which people, equipment, materials, and information are intertwined, as a single **system** and studies how to make it run better. The factories, shops, and figures in this course are all hypothetical, made up to explain concepts. They are not guidelines for judging real equipment or sites.

The simplest frame for understanding a system has three boxes.
- **Input**: what comes in, such as materials, people's time, and orders.
- **Transformation**: the work that turns inputs into something of value, such as processing, assembly, cooking, or packing.
- **Output**: what goes out, such as products or services.

**Feedback** is added to this frame. It is a loop that sends the results of the output (customer reactions, remaining inventory, number of defects) back to the front, to adjust the next inputs and transformations. Without feedback, a system repeats the same work without knowing how it is doing.

explain.alt: Three boxes labeled from left to right 'Input' (materials, orders), 'Transformation' (cooking, packing), and 'Output' (lunch boxes) are connected by arrows. An orange line starts below the output box, runs left, and returns to the input box. Beneath the line is written 'Feedback: customer reactions, remaining inventory'.

explain: A habit that stands out in industrial engineering is to **look at the whole first**. If you speed up only one step while the others stay the same, the overall performance barely increases. Making one part as good as possible (**local optimization**) can differ from making the whole as good as possible.
A simple value often used to describe performance is the **yield**. It is the proportion of the input that becomes usable output: yield = number of good units ÷ number of units input × 100 (%).

body: In a hypothetical bakery, flour and order slips are the inputs, baking the dough is the transformation, and the finished bread is the output. If the baker adjusts the amount of dough the next day based on customers' comments, that is feedback.
Even if the oven is replaced with one twice as fast, if only one person is packing, bread simply piles up at the packing stage. The bakery's total daily sales barely increase.

ie-02.title: Work measurement and standard time
explain: To improve work, you first need to know how long it takes. **Work measurement** is the task of timing a job and setting a reference value from those times. That value is the **standard time**. It is used to calculate process capacity and to plan schedules. The numbers in this course are all hypothetical.

The most basic method is to time the same task several times with a stopwatch. A single measurement fluctuates a lot by chance, so take several measurements and average them. This average is the **observed time**.

explain.alt: A bar chart titled 'Observed time (seconds)'. The bars for runs 1 through 5 have the numbers 38, 42, 40, 41, and 39 above them. A single orange dotted line runs horizontally across the chart and is labeled 'average' at its right end.

explain: However, the observer may have been faster or slower than usual. So a **rating factor** (rating) is multiplied in to convert the time into the time it would have taken at a normal pace. This is the **normal time**. If the observer judges the work to be 10 % faster than normal, the rating factor is 1.10.
$$\text{정상 시간} = \text{관측 평균} \times \text{평가 계수}$$

People cannot work without pause. An **allowance** must be added for fatigue, personal needs, and unavoidable delays. Here the allowance rate is defined as a ratio to the normal time. If the allowance rate is $0.25$, it works out as follows.
$$\text{표준 시간} = \text{정상 시간} \times (1 + \text{여유율})$$

Once the standard time is set, plans can be made. If the standard time is 50 seconds, the benchmark rate is $3600 \div 50 = 72$ units in one hour (3600 seconds). Standard time is only a benchmark for calculating schedules and capacity; it is not a value for measuring a person's worth.

The normal time is $30 \times 0.90 = 27$ seconds. If the allowance rate is $0.20$, the standard time is $27 \times 1.20 = 32.4$ seconds.

ie-03.title: Process and bottleneck
explain: A **process** is a sequence of steps through which work flows. In a process where steps follow one another, each step receives what the previous step has finished. The time each step takes to handle one item is called the **processing time**. The numbers in this course are hypothetical.

explain.alt: Boxes for Process 1 'Cutting' at 30 seconds per unit, Process 2 'Assembly' at 45 seconds per unit, and Process 3 'Inspection' at 36 seconds per unit, from left to right, are connected by arrows. Below them is written 'Processing time per unit'.

explain: Consider three steps as in the figure above: cutting, assembly, and inspection. The step that makes the flow of items slowest is called the **bottleneck**. The bottleneck is the step with the longest processing time. Downstream steps can only receive what the bottleneck passes on, and upstream steps, however fast they are, only matter up to the amount the bottleneck can take in.
The maximum number of items the process can produce per hour is the **throughput**. Divide the 3600 seconds in one hour by the bottleneck's processing time (seconds per unit).
$$\text{처리량(개/시간)} = \dfrac{3600}{\text{병목의 처리 시간(초/개)}}$$

Improving the bottleneck increases throughput, but speeding up a step that is not the bottleneck hardly changes throughput. It is also common that once the bottleneck is improved, the next slowest step becomes the new bottleneck.

The total time from when an item enters the process until it leaves is the **lead time**. It includes waiting time as well as working time. The average number of unfinished items inside the process is called **work in process** (WIP). When the process is stable, the following relationship holds. This is called Little's law.
$$\text{재공품} = \text{처리량} \times \text{리드타임}$$

If assembly is reduced to 30 seconds, the longest processing time becomes inspection's 36 seconds. The new throughput is $3600 \div 36 = 100$ units/hour. No matter how much more assembly is reduced, to exceed 100 units, inspection must be improved.

ie-04.title: Inventory and order quantity
explain: **Inventory** is the goods piled up in a warehouse at a given time. Inventory acts as a buffer that fills the time gap when demand and supply do not match. However, holding inventory also costs money. The numbers in this course are hypothetical.

Two kinds of cost are involved in inventory.
- **Ordering cost**: the fixed cost of placing one order. The more you order at once, the fewer orders you place, so the total ordering cost decreases.
- **Holding cost**: the cost of keeping inventory on hand. The more you order at once, the higher the average inventory, so the total holding cost increases.

For simplicity, assume that you order $Q$ units at a time, demand is constant, and the goods are used up at a steady rate. Then inventory forms a sawtooth shape, as in the figure. When an order arrives, the level rises to $Q$, and it falls to 0 as the goods are used. The average inventory is then $Q \div 2$.

explain.alt: A graph titled 'Warehouse inventory level'. The top of the vertical axis is marked '100 units' and the bottom is 0. Inventory starts at 100, falls in a straight line to 0, and at the point marked by a dotted line 'Order arrives' jumps back up to 100 and falls in the same shape once more. 'Time' is written at the end of the horizontal axis.

explain: If the annual demand is $D$, the ordering cost per order is $S$, and the cost of holding one unit for one year is $H$, the annual cost is as follows.
$$\text{총비용} = \dfrac{D}{Q} \times S + \dfrac{Q}{2} \times H$$
The two terms move in opposite directions as $Q$ grows. The order quantity that makes the sum smallest is called the **economic order quantity**. Under the simple assumptions above, it is as follows.
$$Q^{*} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2DS}{H}}$$

The period from placing an order until the goods arrive is the **lead time**. Demand continues during that time, so an order must be placed when inventory has fallen to the **demand during lead time** for the goods to arrive in time. This inventory level is the reorder point. Because real demand fluctuates, a **safety stock** is often added to guard against shortages.

examples.title: Comparing order quantities of 100 and 200
body: Suppose a hypothetical part is used at an annual rate of $D = 400$ units, with ordering cost $S = 50$ and holding cost $H = 4$.

With $Q = 100$, the ordering cost is $400 \div 100 \times 50 = 200$ and the holding cost is $100 \div 2 \times 4 = 200$, so the total cost is 400. With $Q = 200$, the ordering cost is $100$ and the holding cost is $400$, so the total cost is 500. The cost is lowest at the economic order quantity $\sqrt{2 \times 400 \times 50 \div 4} = 100$.

ie-05.title: Quality and control charts
explain: **Quality** is the degree to which something fits its intended use. In industrial engineering, quality is judged by measured values and defect counts rather than by feel. The simplest such value is the **defect rate**.
$$\text{불량률} = \dfrac{\text{불량 수}}{\text{검사 수}} \times 100\ (\%)$$

Even when the same machine makes the same part, the dimensions vary slightly. Variation is divided into two kinds.
- **Common cause**: small fluctuations that are always present. They occur even when the process is stable.
- **Special cause**: a change with a specific reason, such as new raw material, tool wear, or a change in settings.

A **control chart** is a graph that plots measured values in time order to judge whether variation comes from a common cause or a special cause. It has a **center line** (the average) and **control limits** above and below it. The upper one is called the **UCL** and the lower one the **LCL**. This course covers only the simplest case, which plots individual measurements. When the process is stable and the spread of the values is $\sigma$ (standard deviation), the limits are set as follows.
$$\text{UCL} = \text{평균} + 3\sigma, \quad \text{LCL} = \text{평균} - 3\sigma$$

explain.alt: A control chart titled 'Individual measurements (mm)'. An orange dotted line at the top marks the UCL, a solid green line in the middle marks the center line, and an orange dotted line at the bottom marks the LCL. Points numbered 1 to 12 are connected by lines. Most lie near the center line, but only point 9 is above the UCL line, and it is larger and orange.

explain: If the values follow a normal distribution, about 99.7 % of them lie between these two lines. So a point outside the lines is hard to attribute to chance, and it is read as a **signal** to look for a cause.

There is one caveat. The control limits are set from the spread that the process itself shows, and they are separate from the **specification limits** that customers require. A point within the control limits does not guarantee that the product meets specifications, and a point outside the control limits does not mean that the product is immediately defective.

If one piece measures 50.7 mm on a certain day, it is above the UCL, which is a signal to check whether a special cause occurred. Start by checking, for example, whether a new batch of raw material was introduced that day.

ie-06.title: Decision making under uncertainty
explain: Decisions such as whether to expand a factory or buy equipment must be made without knowing what will happen. The frame for organizing such decisions has four parts: **alternatives** (the choices you can make), **states** (what may happen in the future), **probabilities** (how likely each state is), and **payoffs** (the result, a gain or a loss, for each combination of alternative and state). The numbers in this course are hypothetical.

explain.alt: From a rectangle on the left, two branches labeled 'A expand' and 'B maintain' go out, each leading to a circle. A expand splits into 'high 0.4: +100' and 'low 0.6: −40'. B maintain splits into 'high 0.4: +30' and 'low 0.6: +10'. Below is written 'Unit: million won (hypothetical)'.

explain:
The figure above is a hypothetical equipment investment decision. The probability that demand is high is 0.4, and the probability that it is low is 0.6. The probabilities always sum to 1. Payoffs are in units of million won.
- A expand: +100 if high, −40 if low
- B maintain: +30 if high, +10 if low

The value obtained by multiplying each alternative's payoff in each state by that state's probability and adding the results is the **expected value**. It can be understood as the average payoff when the same decision is repeated many times.
$$\text{기대값} = \sum (\text{확률} \times \text{보수})$$
The expected value of A is $0.4 \times 100 + 0.6 \times (-40) = 16$, and that of B is $0.4 \times 30 + 0.6 \times 10 = 18$. By expected value, B is slightly better.

But expected value is not the whole of a decision. For a one-time decision, you must also consider whether you can bear a large loss and what happens if the probability estimate is wrong. Checking whether the ranking flips when the probabilities change slightly is called **sensitivity analysis**.

examples.title: When the probabilities change

A becomes $0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times (-40) = 30$, and B becomes $0.5 \times 30 + 0.5 \times 10 = 20$. The ranking has flipped. This result does not show which option is right; it shows how sensitive the conclusion is to the probability estimates.

ie-07.title: Linear programming modeling
explain: A factory makes several products using limited machine time, raw materials, and labor. What quantities should be made to maximize profit? **Resource allocation** problems like this can be turned into mathematical models, and **linear programming** (LP) is the tool that finds the optimal solution. It is a starting point of industrial engineering and management science, and it is used for airline scheduling, feed blending, and logistics delivery planning.

The three elements of a linear programming model are: (1) **decision variables**, the values we choose (the production $x$ of product A and $y$ of product B); (2) the **objective function**, the value to maximize or minimize (profit $3x + 5y$); and (3) **constraints**, the limits that cannot be exceeded (machine time $3x + 2y \le 18$), usually together with nonnegativity conditions ($x, y \ge 0$). Because the objective and the constraints are both **first-degree expressions** in the variables, the model is called "linear."

Modeling tips: first write the problem in words ("Process 1 can be used for only 4 hours a week, and one unit of A takes 1 hour"). Next, match the units (hours with hours, kg with kg). Then list every decision variable and constraint without omission. Common mistakes are leaving out the nonnegativity conditions, adding quantities with different units, and swapping "at least" (≥) with "at most" (≤).

The assumptions of linear programming and what they mean: **proportionality** (producing twice as much doubles profit and resource use), **additivity** (the profits and resource use of the products simply add up), **divisibility** (decision variables may be fractions), and **certainty** (all coefficients are known exactly). With bulk discounts, proportionality breaks; with synergies between products, additivity breaks; and when the answer must be a whole number, such as the number of airplanes, divisibility breaks. When integer conditions are needed, **integer programming** is used, which is generally much harder to solve (NP-complete, a topic from the second stage of computer science).

Limitations: a model is a simplification of reality. If the coefficients are estimates, the optimal solution also depends on those estimates, so you must look at how the solution changes when the coefficients change (sensitivity analysis, lesson 3). In addition, if there are goals other than profit, such as quality, employee burden, or the environment, they are hard to capture in a single objective function. This lesson is conceptual and is not practical advice for production planning.

examples.title: Turning words into a model
body: Conditions (hypothetical): a furniture workshop makes chairs (profit 30,000 won) and tables (50,000 won). Process 1 (cutting) is available 4 hours a week and needs 1 hour per chair only. Process 2 (assembly) is available 12 hours a week and needs 2 hours per table only. Process 3 (finishing) is available 18 hours a week and needs 3 hours per chair and 2 hours per table.
Step 1: let the variable $x$ be the number of chairs and $y$ the number of tables. Maximize the objective $3x + 5y$ (in units of 10,000 won).
Step 2: constraints $x \le 4$, $2y \le 12$, $3x + 2y \le 18$, and $x, y \ge 0$. We solve this model in the next lesson.

ie-08.title: The graphical method and the principle of the simplex method
explain: A linear program with two variables can be solved graphically. Once you understand the graphical method, the principle of the **simplex method**, by which a computer solves problems with thousands of variables, follows naturally. The key insight is that "the optimal solution always lies at a **vertex**."

explain.alt: Linear programming figure. The horizontal axis is x (product A, 0 to 7) and the vertical axis is y (product B, 0 to 10). The constraints x ≤ 4 (vertical dotted line), y ≤ 6 (horizontal dotted line), and 3x + 2y ≤ 18 (slanted dotted line) are drawn. The vertices of the shaded polygon they enclose are marked O(0, 0), P(4, 0), Q(4, 3), R(2, 6), and S(0, 6).

explain: Graphical method: (1) draw each constraint as a line and mark the side that satisfies it. (2) Find the region that satisfies all the constraints at once, the **feasible region**. A region formed by linear constraints is a convex polygon. (3) The objective function $3x + 5y = c$ is a line that shifts in parallel depending on the value of $c$. Push this line in the direction of increasing $c$ as far as possible while it still touches the feasible region. The point where it last touches is the optimal solution.

Because the objective function is linear and the region is convex, the optimal solution lies at a vertex (if the objective line is parallel to one side, the entire side can be optimal). So it suffices to compare the objective values at the vertices. In the figure, O gives 0, P gives 12, Q gives 27, R gives 36, and S gives 30, so R(2, 6) is optimal, with a maximum profit of 36.

The **simplex method** extends this idea to higher dimensions. It starts from one vertex and keeps moving to a **neighboring vertex** that improves the objective function, and it stops when no neighbor improves it further. Thanks to convexity, if no neighbor is better, the point is optimal overall (local optimum = global optimum). The number of vertices can be enormous, but in practice the optimum is usually reached after a small number of moves.

Special cases: **infeasible** (the constraints contradict one another, so the region is empty), **unbounded** (the objective can be increased without limit, a sign that a constraint was left out), and **multiple optimal solutions** (the objective line is parallel to one side). Limitation: because the optimum lies at a vertex, extreme solutions that use up some resources exactly tend to appear. A small error in a coefficient can shift the solution to another vertex, so sensitivity analysis is important.

ie-09.title: Duality and shadow prices
explain: If the factory in the previous lesson could secure one more hour of finishing process time, how much would profit increase? And how much money could be paid at most for that one hour? Along with the optimal solution, linear programming gives the answer to such questions: the **shadow price**. The foundation for this is **duality**.

A **shadow price** is the amount by which the optimal objective value increases when the right-hand side (the amount of a resource) of one constraint is increased by one unit. The shadow price of a resource that has **slack** (is not fully used) at the optimum is 0, because giving more of it would not be used. Only a **binding** (fully used) resource has a positive shadow price. This relationship is called **complementary slackness**.

In the previous example, the optimal solution (2, 6) fully uses processes 2 and 3, and process 1 has slack. The shadow price of process 1 is 0. If the time of process 3 is increased by 1 to 19, the new optimal point, found by solving $2y = 12$ and $3x + 2y = 19$, is $(7/3, 6)$, and the profit is $7 + 30 = 37$. The shadow price is 1 (10,000 won per hour). If process 2 is increased by 1, the solution moves to $(5/3, 6.5)$, giving $5 + 32.5 = 37.5$, with a shadow price of 1.5.

**Dual problem**: every maximization LP (the primal problem) has a paired minimization LP. If the primal asks 'maximize profit from resources,' the dual asks 'what is the lowest price a buyer would be willing to pay for each resource.' The dual variables are exactly the shadow prices. **Strong duality theorem**: the optimal values of the two problems are equal. In the previous example, $0 \times 4 + 1.5 \times 12 + 1 \times 18 = 36$, which matches the optimal value of the primal problem.

Uses and limitations: the shadow price is the benchmark for judging whether additional resources are worth buying. If the hourly cost of outsourcing process 3 is less than 10,000 won, buying is profitable. However, a shadow price is valid **only within a certain range**. If you keep increasing a resource, another constraint becomes binding, the optimal vertex changes, and the shadow price changes as well. Examining this range of validity together is **sensitivity analysis**.

ie-10.title: Poisson process and the exponential distribution
explain: The times at which customers arrive at a bank counter, calls come into a call center, and machines break down cannot be predicted. Yet random events also follow statistical regularities. This lesson covers the **Poisson process** and the **exponential distribution**, which form the basis of queueing and reliability analysis (an extension of the Poisson distribution from statistics stage 2 along the time axis).

A process in which events occur independently at a constant average rate $\lambda$ (average number per unit time) is called a **Poisson process**. The number of events in an interval of length $t$ follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda t$. $P(N = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}$.

The **interval** between one event and the next follows an **exponential distribution**. The probability that the interval is longer than $t$ is $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, and the mean interval is $1/\lambda$. If an average of 6 people arrive per hour, that is one person every 10 minutes on average. The most distinctive property of the exponential distribution is **memorylessness**. Even if you have already waited 10 minutes, the distribution of the remaining waiting time is the same as it was at the start. The past does not affect the future.

Applications: customer arrivals, phone calls, radioactive decay, and chance failures of electronic parts are typical Poisson processes. In reliability engineering, if the failure rate $\lambda$ is constant, the probability of not failing by time $t$ (**reliability**) is $R(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, and the mean time between failures (MTBF) is $1/\lambda$. When several independent parts are connected in **series** (if even one fails, the whole fails), their failure rates add.

Limitations: the core of the Poisson process is the assumption that the rate is constant and the events are independent. If customers crowd in at lunchtime, the rate changes over time, and when group customers arrive together, they are not independent. A machine wears out with long use, its failure rate rises, and memorylessness no longer holds (the wear-out failure section of the bathtub curve). Assumptions must be checked against data.

ie-11.title: The M/M/1 queue and Little's law
explain: Nobody likes waiting in line. How many counters should be opened? How much should the server's processing speed be increased? **Queueing theory** takes into account the randomness of arrivals and service and computes average waiting times and queue lengths. The most basic model is **M/M/1**.

M/M/1 is a single-server queue in which arrivals form a Poisson process (average arrival rate $\lambda$; M stands for memoryless), and service times are exponential (average service rate $\mu$). The **utilization** $\rho = \lambda/\mu$ is the fraction of time the server is busy. For the queue not to grow without limit, $\rho < 1$ is needed; that is, the processing speed must be faster than the arrival speed.

Main formulas (steady state): the average number of customers in the system $L = \frac{\rho}{1 - \rho}$, the average number waiting in line $L_q = \frac{\rho^2}{1 - \rho}$, the time in the system $W = \frac{1}{\mu - \lambda}$, and the waiting time $W_q = \frac{\rho}{\mu - \lambda}$. These are connected by **Little's law** $L = \lambda W$, $L_q = \lambda W_q$ (the same law seen in business stage 3).

explain.alt: The horizontal axis is utilization ρ = λ/μ (0 to 1), and the vertical axis is the average number of customers in the system L (0 to 20). The curve is almost flat when ρ is small and shoots up sharply as it approaches 1. The points (0.5, 1), (0.8, 4), and (0.9, 9) are marked.

explain: The most important lesson is the **nonlinearity** shown in the figure. At 50 % utilization the average is 1 customer, at 80 % it is 4, at 90 % it is 9, and at 95 % it is 19. As utilization approaches 1, waiting grows explosively. So running the server '100 % busy' may look efficient on cost, but customer waiting becomes unbearable. A system with randomness needs **spare capacity**.

Limitations: the assumption of exponential service times is the case in which service times vary greatly. If service times are constant (M/D/1), waiting drops to about half. In other words, **variability itself creates waiting**. For multiple servers (M/M/c), or when customers leave if the line gets long, other formulas are used. This lesson covers concepts and calculations.

ie-12.title: Monte Carlo simulation
explain: The formulas from the previous lesson can be used only under simple assumptions. Real factories involve machine breakdowns, worker shift changes, multistage processes, and priority rules that cannot be solved with formulas. In such cases, the method of **imitating** random events on a computer countless times to obtain the distribution of results is **Monte Carlo simulation**.

Basic procedure: (1) build a **model** of the system (what is random, and by what rules it moves). (2) Determine the **probability distribution** of the inputs (interarrival times follow an exponential distribution, and processing times follow the distribution of the data). (3) Draw input values using **random numbers** and run the system once (one **replication**). (4) Repeat thousands to tens of thousands of times and collect the distribution of the outputs (average waiting time, daily production). (5) Calculate the mean and the confidence interval.

The basic method for producing a desired distribution from random numbers is the **inverse transform method**. Draw a uniform random number $U$ between 0 and 1 and substitute it into the inverse of the cumulative distribution function. For an exponential distribution, $T = -\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln U$. For a discrete distribution, the value is set by which cumulative-probability interval $U$ falls in (for example, if $U < 0.3$ then 'failure,' otherwise 'normal').

The precision of the result depends on the number of replications. According to the central limit theorem from statistics stage 2, the standard error of the simulation mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. To double the precision, you must increase the number of replications fourfold. So results are reported together with a **confidence interval** rather than as a single number. Comparing several alternatives using the same sequence of random numbers (common random numbers) lets you see the differences between alternatives more precisely.

Limitations: a simulation is meaningful **only when the model is correct** (garbage in, garbage out). Verify the input distributions against real data, and **validate** the model by comparing its results with theoretical formulas for simple cases. Also, a simulation answers 'what happens if we do this,' but it does not directly find the optimal value. You must build several alternatives and compare them.

examples.title: Generating interarrival times by the inverse transform
body: Conditions: average interarrival time of 5 minutes ($\lambda = 0.2$/minute), random number $U = 0.5$.
Step 1: $T = -5\ln 0.5 = 5 \times 0.693 \approx 3.47$ minutes.
Step 2: if $U = 0.1$, $T = -5\ln 0.1 \approx 11.5$ minutes. The smaller $U$ is, the longer the interval. Repeating with many values of $U$ brings the average close to 5 minutes.

examples.title: Replications and precision
body: Conditions: the standard deviation of a single simulation result is 20 minutes, and there are 1,000 replications.
Step 1: standard error of the mean $= 20/\sqrt{1000} \approx 0.63$ minutes, and the 95% confidence interval is about ±1.24 minutes.
Step 2: to narrow the confidence interval to ±0.62 minutes, 4,000 replications are needed.

ie-13.title: Newsvendor model: the optimal quantity for a single order
explain: A newsstand brings in the newspapers it will sell today once, in the morning. Leftovers become waste, and shortages mean lost sales. The model for choosing the optimal order quantity in situations where you can order **only once and demand is uncertain**, such as fashion clothing, holiday gift sets, or a bakery's daily production, is the **newsvendor model**. It is a different problem from the EOQ model (repeated ordering) covered in the first stage.

Compare two costs. **Underage cost** $C_u$: the profit lost by being one unit short (selling price − purchase cost). **Overage cost** $C_o$: the loss incurred by having one unit left over (purchase cost − salvage value). In **marginal analysis**, you decide whether to order one more unit: if $p$ is the probability that this one extra unit will sell, compare the expected gain $pC_u$ with the expected loss $(1 - p)C_o$.

최적 주문량 $Q^*$는 수요가 $Q^*$ 이하일 확률이 **임계 비율**과 같아지는 수량이다. $$P(D \le Q^*) = \frac{C_u}{C_u + C_o}$$ 부족 비용이 과잉 비용보다 크면 임계 비율이 0.5보다 커서 평균 수요보다 **많이** 주문하고, 반대면 **적게** 주문한다. 수요가 정규분포 $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$이면 $Q^* = \mu + z\sigma$이고, $z$는 임계 비율에 해당하는 표준정규 값이다(통계학 2단계).

Let's check the intuition. A premium cake with a large profit per piece (a big gain when it sells, but discarded if left over) has a large underage cost, so you make plenty. A product with a small margin, where leftovers are costly, is ordered conservatively. If leftover goods can be sold at a discount (the salvage value rises), the overage cost falls, so you may order more.

Limitations: the model assumes that you know the demand distribution. When the distribution is estimated from past sales, the sales on days when the product sold out are smaller than true demand (censored data), so demand is easily underestimated. Also, if a stockout loses customers in the long run, that loss must be added to the underage cost. This lesson is conceptual and is not practical advice for ordering.

Step 1: $C_u = 2$, $C_o = 1$, critical ratio $= 2/3 \approx 0.667$, $z \approx 0.43$.
Step 2: $Q^* \approx 100 + 0.43 \times 20 \approx 109$ units. Prepare more than the average.

ie-14.title: MRP and JIT: push and pull
explain: A single car uses tens of thousands of parts. Once the production plan for finished cars is set, when and how much of each part should be prepared? There are two representative production management philosophies: MRP, which **pushes** by making things in advance according to a plan, and JIT, which **pulls** in response to actual consumption.

**Material requirements planning** (MRP) starts from the finished-product production plan (the **master production schedule**). Using the **bill of materials** (BOM: which parts, and how many of each, go into one finished product), **inventory records**, and **lead times**, it calculates when and how much of each part to order or produce. The calculation is stepwise: gross requirements → **net requirements** after subtracting current inventory and scheduled receipts → the **order release** timing, moved earlier by the lead time.

Demand for parts is calculated **dependently** from the finished-product plan. If 100 bicycles are made, exactly 200 wheels are needed, so there is no need to forecast the demand for wheels separately. This is the strength of MRP. On the other hand, if the plan is wrong or lead times fluctuate, inventory builds up or runs short, which is its weakness.

**Just-in-time production** (JIT) is a philosophy that came from the Toyota Production System: make only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. It is a **pull** system in which the upstream process remakes only what the downstream process takes, and signals are sent by **kanban** (cards). The key is not simply to reduce inventory, but to expose and fix the problems (defects, breakdowns, long setup times) that inventory had been hiding. Inventory is compared to 'water hiding the rocks beneath the surface of a river.'

Limitations and choices: JIT works well when demand is stable, suppliers are nearby, and quality and equipment are stable. When the supply chain is long and uncertain (overseas parts, disasters), a JIT with little inventory is exposed to great risk. Real companies mix methods, for example by making large plans with MRP while running the shop floor on JIT principles. This lesson is conceptual and is not practical advice for production planning.

ie-15.title: CPM and PERT: project schedule management
explain: A project to build a building or launch a new product has tens to thousands of tasks, and some tasks cannot start until others finish. How many days will the project take at minimum, and if a task is late, will the whole project be late? **CPM** (critical path method) and **PERT** answer these questions.

explain.alt: Project network. From the start, the network splits into A (3 days) and B (4 days). After A comes C (2 days), and after B comes D (5 days). E (3 days) can start only when both C and D are finished, and E is the end.

explain: The project is drawn as a **network**. Each task is a node, and precedence relationships are shown by arrows. Among all the paths from start to end, the **longest path** determines the minimum completion time of the project. This path is called the **critical path**. In the figure, path A-C-E takes $3 + 2 + 3 = 8$ days and path B-D-E takes $4 + 5 + 3 = 12$ days, so the critical path is B-D-E and the project duration is 12 days.

The **slack time** (slack) of each task is the time by which that task can be delayed without delaying the overall duration. A task on the critical path has zero slack: even one day of delay delays the whole project by one day. In the figure, A and C have slack of $12 - 8 = 4$ days. The calculation finds the **earliest start and finish times** by going forward from the beginning, and the **latest start and finish times** by going backward from the end, and obtains the slack from the difference.

**PERT** estimates three values when task times are uncertain: the optimistic time $a$, the most likely time $m$, and the pessimistic time $b$. It approximates the mean as $\frac{a + 4m + b}{6}$ and the variance as $\left(\frac{b - a}{6}\right)^2$, and adds the means and variances of the tasks on the critical path to obtain the distribution of the project duration (approximately normal). This makes it possible to calculate 'the probability of finishing within 30 days.'

**Schedule compression** (crashing): to shorten the duration, tasks on the critical path must be shortened. Shortening a task that has slack costs money but does not shorten the duration. As you keep shortening critical-path tasks, another path may become the new critical path. Limitation: PERT's normal approximation assumes a single critical path, but if several paths have nearly the same length, the actual probability of delay is higher. Resource constraints such as manpower also affect the schedule.

ie-16.title: Statistical quality control: control charts
explain: In stage 1 we looked at the basic concept of control charts. This time we treat quantitatively how to build and read control charts in practice. The key question is whether the variation seen now is the process's **natural fluctuation**, or a **special cause** that has arisen and must be fixed.

Shewhart divided variation into two kinds. **Common cause** (chance cause): variation produced by the sum of many small factors that are always present in the process. If only this exists, the process is **in control**. **Special cause** (assignable cause): specific causes that can be found and removed, such as tool wear, a change of raw-material lot, or a change of operator. A control chart is a tool for distinguishing between the two kinds of variation.

**$\bar{X}$-R control chart**: at fixed intervals, draw samples of size $n$ (for example, 5) and record the sample mean $\bar{X}$ and the range $R$. The center line is the overall mean $\bar{\bar{X}}$, and the control limits are $\bar{\bar{X}} \pm 3\sigma_{\bar{X}}$. The standard deviation of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ (central limit theorem). In practice, the average range $\bar{R}$ and a table coefficient are used: $\bar{\bar{X}} \pm A_2\bar{R}$ (for $n = 5$, $A_2 = 0.577$). The **p control chart**, which monitors the defect rate, has limits $\bar{p} \pm 3\sqrt{\bar{p}(1 - \bar{p})/n}$.

Rules for judging an **out-of-control signal**: (1) one point outside the control limits; (2) 7 to 9 consecutive points on one side of the center line (a shift in the mean); (3) 6 or more consecutive points steadily rising or falling (a trend, such as from tool wear); (4) a periodic pattern. When the process is in control, a point outside the control limits (±3σ) appears by chance only about 0.27 % of the time, so when one appears, its cause is investigated.

An important distinction: **control limits are not specification limits.** Control limits come from how the process actually behaves, while specification limits come from what the customer requires. A process that is in control can still fail to meet specifications (process capability, in the next lesson). Also, reacting to every single point by adjusting a process that is in control actually increases the variation (over-adjustment). Limitation: the 3σ criterion is a compromise between false alarms and missed signals (Type I and Type II errors in statistics), and small shifts in the mean are detected late.

Step 2: upper control limit 51.15 mm, lower control limit 48.85 mm. If a later sample mean is 51.3, it is an out-of-control signal, so the cause is investigated.

ie-17.title: Process capability index and design of experiments
explain: How well can an in-control process meet the customer's specifications? And to improve the process, which factors should be changed? The **process capability index** answers the first question, and **design of experiments** answers the second.

explain.alt: Figure of the distribution of part diameters (mm) and the specification limits. Vertical lines mark the lower specification limit at 9.0 and the upper specification limit at 11.0, and a dotted line marks the target at 10.0. The bell-shaped distribution is labeled with a mean of 10.2 and a standard deviation of 0.2, so the distribution is shifted to the right of the target.

explain: The **process capability index** $C_p = \frac{USL - LSL}{6\sigma}$ is the ratio of the specification width to the process's spread of variation (±3σ = 6σ). It is the potential capability when the process is centered within the specifications. If the actual mean is off-center, $C_{pk} = \min\left(\frac{USL - \mu}{3\sigma}, \frac{\mu - LSL}{3\sigma}\right)$ is used, which looks at the distance to the nearer specification limit. Commonly, $C_{pk} \ge 1.33$ is considered good, and below 1 is considered incapable. In the figure, $C_p = 2/(6 \times 0.2) \approx 1.67$, but because the mean is 0.2 off-center, $C_{pk} = (11.0 - 10.2)/0.6 \approx 1.33$.

If $C_p$ is high but $C_{pk}$ is low, improvement comes just from **moving the mean** (adjustment). If $C_p$ itself is low, a fundamental improvement that **reduces the variation** is needed. The method for finding which factors affect the variation and the mean is **design of experiments** (DOE).

An experiment that changes only one factor at a time (OFAT) misses the **interaction** between factors. For example, if raising the temperature helps only when the pressure is high, OFAT makes this hard to detect. A **factorial design** systematically tests combinations of levels of several factors. With 2 factors at 2 levels, there are $2^2 = 4$ combinations. The **main effect** of each factor (the change in mean response when that factor's level is changed) and the **interaction effect** are tested with analysis of variance (statistics stage 4). **Randomization** (shuffling the order of trials), **replication**, and **blocking** improve reliability.

Limitations: the process capability index is meaningful only when the distribution is close to normal and the process is in control. If the process is not in control, its performance tomorrow cannot be predicted. When there are many factors, the combinations grow explosively, so a **fractional factorial design** that tests only some of the combinations is used, and the price is that some interactions can no longer be distinguished.

A factorial design tests combinations of levels of several factors at the same time, and estimates the main effects and the interactions together. It also estimates each effect from more of the data for the same number of runs, so it is efficient.

ie-18.title: Ergonomics and work design
explain: However efficient a process is, it will not last if people are easily injured, fatigued, or prone to mistakes. **Ergonomics** is the discipline of designing work, tools, and environments to fit people's physical and cognitive characteristics. Its principle is 'fit the work to the person, not the person to the work.' This lesson covers principles only; it is not industrial safety certification or medical advice.

**Body dimensions**: the height of a workbench, the reach distance of the hands, and the width of passages are set in consideration of the distribution of body dimensions. No single value fits everyone, so design uses **percentiles**. Distances that the hand must reach are designed for a small person (5th percentile), and spaces that must be passed through (door height, knee space) are designed for a large person (95th percentile). Adjustable designs (height-adjustable chairs) accommodate the most people.

**Physical load**: when lifting a heavy object, the strain on the lower back depends greatly not only on the weight but also on the **horizontal distance** from the body to the object (the lever arm). Even with the same weight, lifting it far from the body multiplies the force the back muscles must produce (the torque of mechanical engineering). Repetitive motions, awkward postures, and vibration increase musculoskeletal strain. The basics of design are to set the work height near the elbow, keep objects close to the body, and reduce repetition.

**Cognitive ergonomics**: human attention and memory have limits. Short-term memory can handle only a few chunks at a time. Design principles for reducing mistakes include: layouts that match expectations (**compatibility**: a right-side switch operates the right-side machine), providing feedback, **error-proofing** that makes mistakes hard to make (poka-yoke: connectors that cannot be inserted in the wrong direction), and standardization. In accident investigations, before concluding 'worker carelessness,' check whether a design that induced the mistake existed.

**Connection to work measurement**: adding ergonomics to the standard-time measurement from stage 1 yields an **allowance rate** that accounts for fatigue, as well as rest design. Limitation: ergonomic standards are based on group averages, so individual differences (age, disability, body type) must be considered. The numbers in this lesson are for explaining concepts and are not actual work permissibility criteria.

ie-19.title: Integrated problem solving: improving a hypothetical assembly plant
explain: The first lesson of the capstone analyzes a single hypothetical plant together with the tools from stages 2 to 5. Situation: a small home-appliance assembly plant. Orders average 300 units per day, but production reaches only 250 units per day, the defect rate at finished-product inspection is 6%, and long order waiting times cause strong customer complaints.

**Stage 1 (bottleneck and waiting)**: the hourly processing capacities of the three processes (parts preparation, assembly, and inspection) are 45, 32, and 50 units (360, 256, and 400 units on an 8-hour basis). The bottleneck is assembly. If the arrival of work in front of the assembly process is approximated as Poisson and the processing time as exponential, the utilization is $\rho = 300/(8 \times 32) \approx 1.17 > 1$, so the queue keeps growing. If assembly capacity is raised to 40 per hour, $\rho \approx 0.94$, which is stable but the waiting is very long (if M/M/1, $L \approx 15$). To reach the target utilization of 0.8, about 47 units per hour are needed.

**Stage 2 (resource allocation)**: compare the costs and effects of adding assembly workers and of improving the assembly jig, using linear programming. Under budget and space constraints, find the combination that maximizes the assembly capacity per hour. The shadow price tells the value of a 10,000-won increase in the budget.

**Stage 3 (quality)**: most of the 6% defects were missing screw fastenings in assembly. Looking at the data with a p control chart, defects clustered right after the afternoon shift change (a special cause). Mark the fastening sequence on the jig and install a counting device (poka-yoke), and measure the process capability $C_{pk}$ of the torque in assembly. If defects are filtered out after the bottleneck process, the bottleneck's time is wasted, so placing inspection right after assembly is also worth considering.

**Stage 4 (schedule and critique)**: plan the improvement project as a work network and manage its critical path (jig design → fabrication → testing). **Critique**: the exponential-distribution assumption of the queueing model may differ from the actual variation in assembly times, and it may overestimate waiting. Confirm with a simulation that uses the actual distribution of processing times. Also, the value of investments that reduce utilization should be compared with the value of improved delivery times.

ie-20.title: Capstone: a report on improving a production or service system
explain: The final task is to **choose one hypothetical production or service system, analyze it with at least three of the tools from stages 2 to 5, propose improvements, and critique their assumptions and risks**. Examples: a school cafeteria serving line, a neighborhood clinic reception (not a medical judgment), a parcel sorting area, café order processing, or a library checkout counter.

Report outline: (1) **system and problem definition**: what goes in, what comes out, performance indicators (throughput, waiting time, defect rate, cost), and current figures; (2) **data and assumptions**: arrival rates, processing time distributions, and cost coefficients (hypothetical); (3) **analysis**: at least three of bottleneck and utilization, queueing or simulation, resource allocation (linear programming), inventory and order quantity, quality (control charts and process capability), and ergonomics; (4) **improvement proposal**: concrete measures and their expected effects (in numbers); (5) **execution plan**: the work network and its critical path; (6) **risks and critique**: conditions under which the assumptions break, side effects, and effects on people (workers and customers).

Features of a good report: it finds the bottleneck first. It deals with **variability**, not just averages. It estimates the effects of improvements in numbers and states which assumptions those numbers depend on. It considers not only efficiency but also **people** (fatigue, safety, fairness) and **resilience** (supply disruptions, demand surges).
This task is not graded. The text you submit is stored only on this device, and you can review it later under 'My progress' and 'My notes.'
